vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room of the clinic with his hands folded tightly in his lap, his leg bouncing in a steady, unconscious rhythm. At twenty-six, he has the appearance of someone older—there's a tightness around his eyes, a wariness in how he scans the room before settling into his chair. He works as a bank teller downtown, a job he's held for four years, though lately he finds himself counting down the hours until closing.

Three years ago, Marcus was in the shopping district when the bombing happened. He remembers the ordinary details with crystalline clarity: he was walking toward a café to meet a friend, noticing how the afternoon light caught the storefront windows, thinking about what he might order. Then came the sound—not quite like anything he'd heard before, a compression of air that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The next moments exist in fragments in his mind: the smell of smoke, people screaming, his own body moving without conscious direction, the strange sensation of dust coating his teeth.

He wasn't severely injured. A laceration on his shoulder, some bruising. But thirty-seven people died that day, and Marcus walked away. For months afterward, he was numb, moving through his days with a kind of mechanical efficiency. His wife at the time tried to support him, but he couldn't let her in. He couldn't explain why he'd lie awake at three in the morning listening to the house settle, convinced each creak was a warning of something terrible. By the time she left—eighteen months after the bombing—Marcus barely registered her departure.

Now, when Marcus arrives at the bank each morning, he performs a ritual. He scans the lobby before entering, noting exits, counting how many people are present, assessing who looks suspicious. His manager has noticed he's become hypervigilant with customers, occasionally asking people to leave if they seem agitated or if they're wearing heavy jackets despite the warm weather. Just last week, a woman came in wearing a backpack and Marcus felt his chest tighten so severely he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he sat in a stall for twenty minutes waiting for his breathing to slow.

The nightmares come most nights. In them, he's back in the shopping district, but this time he can't move. He watches people die while his legs remain paralyzed. He wakes gasping, his sheets soaked with sweat, his heart hammering so hard he thinks it might break through his ribs. He's learned not to bother trying to fall back asleep; instead, he sits on his couch in the dark, scrolling through news websites, checking for reports of attacks, unable to stop himself even though the reading only makes things worse.

Alcohol has become a problem. Not dramatically so—he's not missing work or getting arrested—but he's aware that he reaches for a drink most evenings now, that the amount has gradually increased, that the relief it provides is temporary but necessary. His apartment is sparse, decorated minimally, as though he hasn't quite committed to living there. He has no close friends anymore. His family calls, but conversations feel impossible; they want him to "move forward," and he doesn't know how to explain that forward feels like walking toward something that might explode.

What Marcus doesn't say, but what sits beneath everything, is the persistent conviction that he survived by chance, and that chance will eventually run out.
